title: Playing the Blues
description: Six notes and three chords are all you need to start improvising a blues.

steps.title: Six notes
steps.description:
The blues scale is the minor pentatonic with one extra note squeezed in: the flat 5th, often called the blue note. In C that's C, Eb, F, F#, G, Bb.

The F# sits right between F and G. On its own it sounds a little wrong, and that slightly-wrong rub is exactly where the blues lives.

steps.title: The C blues scale
steps.description: Play the six notes from C upward: C, Eb, F, F#, G, Bb. Take it slowly and listen for the moment the F# arrives.
steps.hint: F, F# and G are three keys in a row, white, black, white. That cluster is the heart of the scale.

steps.title: The 12-bar form
steps.description:
Most blues songs, and plenty of rock and roll, repeat the same 12-bar loop built from just three chords, I, IV and V. In C:

• Bars 1-4: C (I)
• Bars 5-6: F (IV)
• Bars 7-8: C (I)
• Bar 9: G (V)
• Bar 10: F (IV)
• Bars 11-12: C (I)

Players often swap that last bar for G to kick off the next time round. Once the loop is in your ears, you'll hear it everywhere.

steps.title: The I chord, C7
steps.description: Blues chords usually carry a flat 7th on top, which gives them that slightly sour, bluesy edge. Play C7: C, E, G and Bb.
steps.hint: Start with a plain C major triad, then add Bb on top. It's the black key just left of B.

steps.title: The IV chord, F
steps.description: Bar 5 moves to F. Play an F major triad: F, A and C. In a real blues you'd often make this F7 as well.
steps.hint: F, A and C are all white keys. Skip one white key between each.

steps.title: The V chord, G
steps.description: Bar 9 is G, the chord with the most pull. Play G, B and D and notice how badly it wants to go back to C.
steps.hint: Same shape as before, all white keys: G, skip A, B, skip C, D.

steps.title: Making it talk
steps.description:
A few things to try when you improvise:

• A piano can't bend notes, so fake it. Slide your finger from F up to F#, or crush the two together and let go of the F.
• Play a short phrase, rest, then answer it, like a question and a reply.
• Land on C or G when you want a phrase to sound finished.
• Mix quick notes with long ones.
• Leave gaps. Silence is part of the line.

The nice part is that this one scale works over all three chords, so you can't really get lost.
